topics.title: Retinoscopy: refinement and the working-distance lens
topics.summary: Retinoscopy gives an objective starting point for the subjective. You neutralise the reflex in each principal meridian, then take off the working-distance allowance: at 67 cm that's 1.50 D, so the net result is the gross result minus +1.50 D.
keyPoints: Working distance allowance = 1 / working distance (m). At 67 cm it's +1.50 D; at 50 cm it's +2.00 D.
Net Rx = gross (lenses in the trial frame at neutral) − working-distance lens. E.g. gross +3.50 at 67 cm → net +2.00.
'With' movement → add plus. 'Against' movement → add minus.
Near neutral the reflex gets brighter, faster and wider; at neutral the pupil fills with no movement.
With a streak retinoscope, find the two principal meridians by rotating the streak until the reflex lines up with it (no 'break').
Patient fixates a distant target with both eyes open (e.g. a green or red target at 6 m) to relax accommodation.
Keep your eyes in line with the patient's visual axis: right eye for their right, left eye for their left.
examTraps: Forgetting to subtract the working-distance lens (or adding it instead).
Recording 'neutral' too early — check by moving slightly forward (should see with) and back (should see against).
Letting the patient look at the light: accommodation creeps in and the result goes too minus.

diagram.description: Three pupils side by side. Left: 'with' movement — the reflex moves the same way as the streak (add plus). Middle: 'against' movement — the reflex moves the opposite way (add minus). Right: neutral — the pupil is filled with a bright reflex and no movement.

goDeeper.heading: Why the working-distance lens exists
goDeeper.body: At neutral, the patient's far point is at your retinoscope's peephole, not at infinity. If you sit at 67 cm, the lenses in the trial frame have made the eye 1.50 D myopic (focused at 67 cm). Taking off +1.50 D gives the Rx that focuses the eye at infinity. Some practitioners put a +1.50 working-distance lens in the frame during ret so the gross reading in the other lenses is already the net result — check which method your clinic expects.

goDeeper.heading: Finding the axis with a streak
goDeeper.body: Sweep the streak at 90° to its length. If the reflex inside the pupil isn't parallel to the streak (it looks 'broken'), rotate the sleeve until they line up: that's a principal meridian. Neutralise it with spheres, then turn the streak 90° and neutralise the other meridian. The difference between the two is the cylinder; its axis is the meridian you neutralised with the more positive sphere when writing the Rx in minus-cylinder form.

goDeeper.heading: Tricky reflexes
goDeeper.body: A dull, slow reflex usually means a large error — try a big lens (±4.00 or more) to find which way you're going. A 'scissors' reflex (two bands moving towards each other) is seen in keratoconus and some high astigmatism. Small pupils and media opacities make the reflex dim; dimming the room and asking the patient to keep looking past you helps.

topics.title: Subjective refraction: best vision sphere, fogging and duochrome
topics.summary: The aim of the spherical part of the subjective is the most plus (least minus) that gives the best acuity. Fogging relaxes accommodation first, then you reduce the plus until vision is best; the duochrome checks you haven't over-minused.
keyPoints: Best vision sphere (BVS) / maximum plus to maximum visual acuity (MPMVA): the most positive sphere that gives the best VA.
Fog first (e.g. +0.75 to +1.00 over the ret result) so accommodation relaxes, then reduce plus in 0.25 D steps.
Each −0.25 D should buy about one line of acuity; if it doesn't, don't give it.
Duochrome: red clearer → add minus (−0.25); green clearer → add plus (+0.25). Aim for equal, or red slightly clearer.
The duochrome works on chromatic aberration, so it still works in most colour vision deficient patients.
Pinhole: if VA improves through a pinhole, the reduced VA is likely refractive.
Use the +1.00 blur test at the end: VA should drop to about 6/12–6/18 (unaided-check of over-minus).
examTraps: Over-minusing: young patients will accept extra minus by accommodating and say it's 'darker/smaller but sharper'.
Reversing the duochrome rule — red clearer means the image is in front of the retina, so add minus.
Forgetting to re-check the sphere after finding the cylinder (maintain the spherical equivalent).

diagram.description: Eye with light entering. Green focus falls in front of red focus because of longitudinal chromatic aberration. Left panel: myopic (under-minused) — red focus nearer retina, red looks clearer, add minus. Right panel: over-minused — green clearer, add plus. Centre: balanced — retina sits between red and green foci (yellow light on the retina).

goDeeper.heading: Why fogging works
goDeeper.body: Putting the eye artificially myopic (fogging) means accommodation can only make things blurrier, so the patient relaxes it. As you reduce the plus, vision improves until you reach the far point. Going past that point the patient has to accommodate to keep things clear, which is why extra minus 'feels' fine to young eyes but causes asthenopia later.

goDeeper.heading: Duochrome in practice
goDeeper.body: Ask: 'Are the letters clearer on the red or the green, or are they the same?' Use the black rings or letters a line above the best VA. Red clearer: add −0.25. Green clearer: add +0.25. If it flips with a single 0.25 step, choose the red-clearer end for younger patients (relaxed accommodation) and the green end can be acceptable for presbyopes doing near work — check your clinic's convention.

goDeeper.heading: Recording the result
goDeeper.body: Record each eye's sphere, cylinder and axis with the VA achieved, e.g. R +1.25/−0.50 × 180 6/5. Note the method (e.g. 'BVS, duochrome balanced') if your clinic asks for it, and the final binocular VA.

topics.title: Jackson cross-cylinder: axis then power
topics.summary: The JCC refines the cylinder: first its axis, then its power. A JCC is a lens with equal and opposite powers in its two meridians (e.g. +0.25/−0.50 × the handle at 45°), flipped to present two choices.
keyPoints: Always refine axis before power — an axis error makes the power look wrong.
Axis check: hold the JCC so its handle lies along the cylinder axis (the JCC axes 'straddle' it at 45°).
Turn the cylinder axis towards the minus axis of the preferred JCC position (when using minus cylinders) — 'follow the red/minus dot'.
Use bigger steps for low cylinders and smaller steps for high cylinders (e.g. 15° for −0.50, 5° for −2.00).
Power check: line up one JCC axis with the cylinder axis. Minus preferred → add −0.25 cyl; plus preferred → reduce cyl by 0.25.
Keep the spherical equivalent: for every −0.50 D cylinder added, add +0.25 DS.
Use a round target (circles or a block of letters one line above best VA).
examTraps: Doing power before axis.
Turning the axis the wrong way (towards the plus axis).
Changing cylinder power without adjusting the sphere to keep the circle of least confusion on the retina.

diagram.description: Circle representing a JCC lens with a handle at 45° to its two principal meridians. One meridian marked with red dots (minus axis), the other white dots (plus axis). Two small panels: 'axis check' with the handle along the trial cyl axis; 'power check' with the red-dot axis aligned to the trial cyl axis.

goDeeper.heading: What the JCC does optically
goDeeper.body: A ±0.25 JCC is +0.25 DS / −0.50 DC. Placed in front of a correctly corrected eye it creates equal blur in both flip positions. If the trial cylinder is off-axis, one position combines with the residual astigmatism to make less blur and the patient prefers it. The preferred minus axis points to where the true axis lies.

goDeeper.heading: Bracketing the axis
goDeeper.body: Move the axis towards the preferred minus axis, check again, and keep going until the preference reverses. Then split the difference ('bracket') until both positions look the same. Patients often find the two choices very similar near the end point — 'they look the same' is a valid answer and usually means you're there.

goDeeper.heading: Finding a cylinder nobody suspected
goDeeper.body: If ret showed no cylinder, check with the JCC at 90/180 and then at 45/135. If the patient consistently prefers a position, put in −0.25 DC at that minus axis and refine axis and power as usual.

Minus preferred: add −0.25 DC (and +0.25 DS for every −0.50 DC added). Plus preferred: reduce cylinder.
Stop when both positions look equal.
Re-check the best vision sphere and record the final result with VA.

topics.title: Binocular balancing, binocular addition and binocular refraction
topics.summary: From Dr Sheppard's week 3 lecture: binocular balancing makes sure accommodation is balanced between the eyes after a monocular subjective. With a trial frame the preferred method is monocular fogging (modified Humphriss). Binocular addition then checks for any extra plus, and binocular refraction does the whole subjective with both eyes open.
keyPoints: Why balance: occluding one eye in monocular refraction can cause proximal accommodation, and an imbalance in the final Rx can cause asthenopia. Balancing equalises accommodation, not vision.

Techniques: monocular fogging (preferred with a trial frame), prism-dissociated blur balance (preferred with a phoropter), Humphriss immediate contrast, and Turville infinite balance (cumbersome, needs a septum).

Monocular fogging: after ret and monocular subjective on both eyes, fog the left with about +0.75 DS and check it reads about 6/12 (add more plus if not). Fogging suppresses central vision but keeps peripheral fusion.

In the right eye add +0.25 while letters are clearer or the same, until VA first blurs. Then try −0.25 and accept it only if letters are clearer, not just smaller and blacker. Repeat with the right eye fogged.

Binocular addition: remove the fog and add +0.25 to both eyes while clearer or the same; useful for low hyperopes with near symptoms. If latent hyperopia is suspected, start with +1.00 both eyes and reduce. A 6 m chart is −0.16 D away, and some patients prefer slightly less plus.
Final Rx = subjective + binocular balance + binocular addition. Record each, plus the +1.00 check test and binocular VA.
Binocular refraction (monocular fogging method): ret both eyes, fog the left with +0.75 (check 6/12), JCC the right, swap, remove fog, binocular addition if needed. No separate balance afterwards.

Binocular refraction suits hyperopia, pseudomyopia and antimetropia, and avoids occlusion effects (pupil dilation, latent nystagmus, cyclophoria). It's hard with a strongly dominant eye and needs a starting point close to the final Rx.
examTraps: Saying binocular balancing equalises vision between the eyes. It balances accommodation.
Choosing monocular refraction for latent nystagmus or cyclophoria: occlusion makes both manifest.
Saying monocular fogging is used for binocular addition: no fog is used, plus goes on both eyes.
Doing a binocular balance after a binocular refraction: it isn't needed.

topics.summary: From the week 4 near vision lecture: when a pre-presbyope has near symptoms, test amplitude (push-up/pull-down), facility (±2.00 flippers) and lag (dynamic retinoscopy), and compare amplitude with the Duane-Hofstetter age norms.
keyPoints: Accommodative dysfunction can be caused by medication, trauma, inflammation, diabetes, Down's syndrome or cerebral palsy, or be idiopathic. Symptoms: headache, eyestrain, near blur, trouble reading or changing focus.

Amplitude by RAF rule with the distance correction on: push the smallest legible print in until blur is sustained (push-up), then pull it out until clear (pull-down), and average the two. Measure R, L and both.
Binocular amplitude is 1–2 D higher than monocular because convergence drives extra accommodation.
Push-up overestimates (depth of focus, print getting bigger, moving target); a −3.00 lens can push the near point out for young patients (then add 3 D to the reading).
Duane-Hofstetter: minimum 15 − 0.25 × age, average 18.5 − 0.30 × age, maximum 25 − 0.40 × age. Suspect accommodative insufficiency if amplitude is more than 1.50 D below expected for age.
Facility with ±2.00 DS flippers at 40 cm: cycles per minute (clearing + and − is one cycle). Fail (up to 30 years): under 11 cpm monocular, under 8 cpm binocular; some suggest 7 and 5 for ages 8–12.
Facility can be abnormal even when amplitude is normal. Lag is measured with dynamic retinoscopy (MEM or modified Nott).

topics.title: Presbyopia and finding the near add
topics.summary: From the week 4 near vision lecture: presbyopia usually starts at 40–45 and true accommodation has gone by about 55. Find a tentative add (preferably from age and working distance), refine it binocularly to the least plus, check the range of clear vision, and record it.
keyPoints: Presbyopia starts earlier in hot climates, people with short arms or close working distances, and hyperopes; later in myopes and long-armed people.
Tentative add, most to least recommended: age and working distance (table), amplitude (add = WD − ½ amp), relative accommodation, binocular cross-cylinder.
Final add: near PD in the trial frame, patient at their own reading distance. Try −0.25 binocularly; if not clearer, try +0.25; stop when clarity no longer improves. This gives the least plus.
Range of clear vision: far end 1 ÷ add, near end 1 ÷ (add + amplitude). Check it by moving the chart in and out; if it doesn't suit, change the add or give an intermediate add.
Adds are usually equal and rarely above +3.00 (except for low vision). Unequal adds may suit amblyopia, lag, anisometropia or a very particular patient.
Don't measure amplitude over 55.
examTraps: Basing the tentative add on measured amplitude: it's error-prone in presbyopes; age and working distance is recommended.
Not checking the range of clear vision at the patient's real working distances.

topics.title: Prescribing decisions and counselling
topics.summary: From Dr Sheppard's week 10 lecture: deciding what to prescribe is 'art rather than science'. Listen to and involve the patient, be careful with plus and minus, big changes and cylinders, think about anisometropia and high powers, only prescribe small errors with good reason, then counsel and record your advice.
keyPoints: Listen: a myope who sees better pushing their glasses closer needs more minus; a hyperope who pushes them away needs more plus; a presbyope reading down the nose needs more add.
Involve the patient: compare old and new in a trial frame or with lenses held over their glasses, and ask whether they'd like new glasses.
'If it ain't broke, don't fix it': a happy patient wanting a new frame is often best with the current Rx. A presbyopic myope may prefer slight distance under-correction.

Myopes: avoid over-plus (6 m chart = +0.17 D; night myopia), err towards slight over-minus. Hyperopes: partial correction (½ to ¾ if manifest) to relieve symptoms; full only for presbyopes, esotropia and esophoria.
Extra minus can decompensate esophoria; extra plus can decompensate exophoria. Recheck binocular vision after a big change, especially with a high AC/A.

Over 25, avoid changes of more than ±0.75 D (stage them). Consider not prescribing 0.25 DC. Make partial cylinder changes over 0.75 DC, or axis changes over 30° (≤1.00 DC), 15° (1.00–2.00 DC) or 7.5° (>2.00 DC); power changes are better tolerated than axis changes.

topics.title: Presbyope clinic: running a full refraction
topics.summary: In the presbyope clinic you put everything together on a real patient: history, vision, retinoscopy, subjective, balancing, near add, range of clear vision, final Rx and advice. Time management and clear communication matter as much as technique.
keyPoints: One session per student between weeks 8 and 12 — check the rota for yours.
Start with a focused history: symptoms, visual tasks and distances, current glasses, health and medication.
Measure habitual VA (distance and near) before changing anything.
Objective (ret) → subjective (BVS, JCC, sphere check) → binocular balance → binocular BVS.
Near add: tentative from age/amplitude, refine binocularly, then check range of clear vision at her real distances.
Trial-frame the final Rx and let her look at her phone or a book before deciding.
Finish with clear advice (lens types, adaptation) and a clear record, signed off by your supervisor.
examTraps: Running out of time on the subjective and rushing the add.
Not measuring habitual VA, so you can't show the improvement.
Prescribing an add without checking the patient's real tasks.

diagram.description: Flowchart of a full refraction: History → Habitual VA → Retinoscopy → Subjective (BVS → JCC → sphere check) → Binocular balance → Binocular BVS → Near add → Range of clear vision → Trial frame check → Advice and recording.

goDeeper.heading: Keeping to time
goDeeper.body: Practise the routine until the order is automatic. A rough split for a teaching clinic might be: history and VAs 10 min, ret 10 min, subjective and balance 20 min, near add and range 10 min, trial frame, advice and records 10 min — your supervisors will tell you the real time limits. If ret is hard, don't get stuck: move on to the subjective.

goDeeper.heading: Talking to a real patient
goDeeper.body: Introduce yourself as a student, explain what you'll do, and get consent. Use plain language ('which is clearer, one or two — or the same?'). Older patients may need more time to answer; don't rush them. Check understanding at the end and invite questions.

goDeeper.heading: What to record
goDeeper.body: Habitual Rx and VAs, ret result, subjective result per eye with VA, binocular VA, add, near VA, range of clear vision, final Rx prescribed and why, advice given, and your supervisor's sign-off.

topics.summary: Near vision adequacy for everyone, accommodation tests when a pre-presbyope has near symptoms, and a structured way to find and check a presbyope's near add.
keyPoints: Near vision adequacy: the smallest N-point paragraph read at the patient's preferred distance, recorded with that distance (e.g. N5 @ 40 cm R, L and Bin).
Amplitude by push-up/pull-down on a RAF rule: average the two end points. Binocular is 1–2 D higher than monocular because convergence drives extra accommodation.
Average expected monocular amplitude = 18.5 − 0.30 × age. Suspect accommodative insufficiency if it is more than 1.50 D below that.
Accommodative facility with ±2.00 flippers at 40 cm: pass is at least 11 cpm monocularly and 8 cpm binocularly (children and adults to 30).
Tentative add: best from age and working distance. From amplitude: add = working distance (D) − ½ amplitude.
Final add: binocular ±0.25 steps, stopping when clarity no longer improves (least plus). Then check the range of clear vision: 1 ÷ (add + amp) to 1 ÷ add.
examTraps: Basing the tentative add on measured amplitude. In presbyopes that measurement is error-prone; age and working distance is the recommended method.
Measuring amplitude in patients over 55: what remains is depth of focus.
Recording an N-number without the working distance.

goDeeper.heading: Why half the amplitude?
goDeeper.body: The amplitude-based formula assumes only about half the amplitude can be sustained comfortably. Research at Aston (Wolffsohn et al., 2011) suggests about 80% may be sustainable, which is one reason this method is less reliable than tables by age and working distance.

goDeeper.heading: When unequal adds are reasonable
goDeeper.body: Amblyopia, accommodative lag, anisometropia (for example after cataract surgery in one eye), or a very particular patient. Before prescribing, recheck the add end points and the distance binocular balance, then check each eye's range and present the result binocularly.

topics.summary: The record is a legal document and the basis of continuity of care. Make it clear, complete, contemporaneous and confidential, and structure it so a reader can follow your reasoning.
keyPoints: GOC outcome 4.12: comply with legal, professional and ethical rules for managing information, including accurate records and confidentiality.

topics.title: Automated refraction
topics.summary: Autorefractors give a quick objective starting point for subjective refraction. Know how they work, when they can mislead, and how to compare their results with subjective findings.
keyPoints: They analyse infrared light reflected from the fundus as an internal optometer lens moves, finding the far point with minimal patient input.
Uses: a starting point for subjective refraction, K readings, and research on accommodation and myopia.
Main error: proximal accommodation (instrument myopia); fogging targets help.
Limits: range about ±25 D, minimum pupil about 2.0–2.9 mm, and some can't measure through cataract (SLD sources cope better than LEDs).
Practice instruments are closed-field; research instruments are open-field.
Compare results with MSE = sphere + cyl/2 and the vector components J0 and J45; use Bland-Altman plots (difference against mean) for agreement and repeatability.
